planting.note: Sow in a nursery bed in autumn and set young plants out on well-drained, terraced slopes in late winter, mimicking the schist 'bancels' of the Cévennes where this onion has been grown for centuries.

directions: Grow this flattened, pale-skinned onion on light, stony, well-drained ground, since it was bred for the terraced hillsides of the Cévennes in Languedoc. It is prized for very low pungency and high sugar content, making it suitable for eating raw in salads or slow-cooked into onion tarts and soups. Keep plants evenly watered through bulb formation but ease off as foliage begins to yellow to improve storage. The variety carries a French AOC designation recognizing its long cultivation history in this part of Occitania.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity Ark of Taste

planting.note: Direct-sow in mid-to-late summer into deep, loose soil so the long black roots can push down undisturbed, then let frost sweeten them before a winter harvest.

directions: This elongated turnip with jet-black skin and dense white flesh is a specialty of the village of Pardailhan in the Hérault hills of Languedoc, grown in a cool, well-drained micro-climate that locals credit for its unusually sweet, nutty flavor. Sow thickly then thin to give roots room to swell, and leave them in the ground well into winter since cold exposure concentrates their sugars. It is traditionally sliced thin and eaten raw with salt, or braised alongside duck and pork in regional Languedoc dishes. The turnip holds Slow Food Ark of Taste recognition for its narrow, single-commune production zone.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity Ark of Taste

planting.note: Start seed indoors in late winter and transplant into rich, irrigated ground near the last frost date, following the practice used along the Adour valley near Tarbes.

directions: A flattened, coppery-skinned sweet onion grown in the alluvial soils around Trébons in the Hautes-Pyrénées, valued for mild flavor and high water content that make it best eaten fresh rather than stored long-term. Give it steady irrigation through the growing season since the sandy river-valley ground it was developed for drains quickly. It is traditionally served raw in salads or lightly grilled alongside regional Gascon dishes. The variety carries French Label Rouge quality recognition tied to its small Pyrenean growing region.

planting.note: Start seed indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost and transplant out once nights stay reliably above 50F, staking lightly since the semi-determinate vines tend to sprawl.

directions: Marmande produces flattened, deeply ribbed beefsteak fruits with mild, low-acid flesh and relatively few seeds, bred around the market-garden town of Marmande on the Garonne in the Occitan-speaking southwest of France. It sets fruit reliably even in cooler, variable spring weather, which made it a favorite among southwestern French growers before glasshouse hybrids took over the market. Use it sliced raw in salads or halved and baked for tomates farcies, a classic regional stuffed-tomato dish. Pinch suckers lightly to keep the sprawling plants manageable without stripping away the character that made this variety a market staple for generations.

planting.note: Start seed indoors eight to ten weeks before the last frost, since germination is slow, and transplant into warm soil only after nights stay reliably above 55F.

directions: Dalle Khursani is a small, round, pea-sized chili from Nepal's mid-hills that ripens from green to a fiery orange-red and packs intense, habanero-range heat on plants that stay compact but bear heavily over a long season. It is the everyday hot pepper of Nepali kitchens, crushed fresh into achar, dried for winter use, or pickled whole in mustard oil. Give it a long, warm growing season and well-drained soil, and expect fruit to continue setting until frost since the plants bear in flushes. Harvest frequently to keep production going, picking some pods green and letting others ripen fully for maximum heat and color.
